responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character08_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well… I reckon Character08_F—she always said “fairness” meant everybody gettin’ a fair shake, not just on paper, but in real life. She didn’t have much formal education, just finished high school back when it was still called that, and she worked most of her life—cleaning offices, helping out at a diner, things like that. So when she talked about fairness, it came from knowin’ what it felt like to be overlooked. Like when the boss would give the easier shifts to folks with connections or younger girls who dressed a certain way—she noticed. And she’d say, “That ain’t fair. We all got mouths to feed.”

She believed belonging wasn’t about where you were born or what your name sounded like—it was about how people treated each other day to day. She grew up in a small town in Ohio, mostly white, mostly poor, everyone knew each other’s business. But she used to say, “Belongin’ don’t mean everybody’s the same. It means you look out for one another.” She remembered during the ’73 strike at the factory—half the workers were Black, half white, but they stood together. That stuck with her. Taught her that community wasn’t about blood or skin color—it was about standin’ side by side when things got hard.

But she also worried sometimes that folks weren’t *really* tryin’ to understand each other anymore. Like, people talk about community, but then move away when someone different moves next door. Or complain about taxes goin’ up while forgettin’ that hospitals and schools help *everyone*, even if they don’t need ‘em right now.

One thing she said often: “You don’t build belonging by wishin’ everyone was like you. You build it by carin’ enough to ask, ‘What do you need?’” She wasn’t preachy about it—just lived it. Took meals to a neighbor with cancer, even though that woman never said more than two words to her before. Sat with another man after his son died in Iraq—didn’t matter that he was Mexican-American and she didn’t speak Spanish. Just brought coffee and sat quiet in the yard.

To her, community was showin’ up. Fairness was makin’ sure others could show up too, without bein’ crushed under the weight of livin’. And belongin’? That was earnin’ the right to call someplace home—not by law or papers, but by care.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character08_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*Sits back a little, hands resting on knees, voice calm but direct*

Well... I’ve been comin’ to this garden every spring since they first put it in, oh, must be fifteen years now. Back then, it was mostly older folks like me—white, born here, some retired, others workin’ part-time jobs that didn’t pay enough. But over the years, more people moved in. You see families from Somalia down the block—their kids always runnin’ through with backpacks too big for ‘em. There’s a Haitian couple runnin’ that little grocery stand now. A Mexican family runs the corner repair shop. And just last year, two young men moved into Mrs. Lang’s old house—they’re gay, live together, both nurses at the county hospital.

At first? Honestly, I’ll say it—I wasn’t sure. Not because I’m afraid of different, but because… well, when you’ve lived one way your whole life, anything new feels strange. Like walkin’ into a room where the furniture’s been moved and you keep stubbin’ your toe.

But then I saw Fatima, that Somali woman, kneelin’ in her plot tryin’ to grow collard greens—same thing my mama used to raise. I walked over and said, “You need more lime in that soil.” She looked up, surprised, then smiled. We ended up talkin’ about how hard it is to get good greens unless you grow ‘em yourself. Next week, she brought me some flatbread, warm from the oven. Tasted like nothing I’d ever had, but I ate it slow and told her it was good—and meant it.

That’s how it started.

Now, I don’t pretend we all think the same. Some folks drink, yeah. Saw Mr. Darnell passed out again near the compost bins last month. Doesn’t mean he’s bad—just broken, like so many of us get after life hits hard. Same with that younger girl, Lena, smokin’ something behind the shed sometimes. I don’t approve, but I also remember what it was like bein’ young and feelin’ like no future waited for you.

What matters is whether we treat each other human. Whether we nod when we pass. Whether we warn someone if their gate’s open or their kid’s chasin’ a ball into the street.

I figure everybody deserves space to belong—even if they don’t talk like me, pray like me, or love like me. Long as they’re not hurtin’ nobody, who am I to decide who fits?

And truth is… this place feels more alive now than when it was all quiet and the same. Kids shoutin’ in two languages, women laughin’ while they pull weeds, even the arguments once in a while—feels real. Feels like people livin’, not just survivin’.

So do I always understand ‘em? No.  
Do I always agree? Lord, no.  
But can I sit beside ‘em, share seeds, maybe borrow a trowel? Yes. That’s startin’ something. That’s buildin’ a neighborhood worth callin’ home.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*Leans forward slightly, hands clasped, voice steady but softer now*

You know… I’ve seen a lot in seventy years. I’ve held my brother’s hand when he died from liver failure—drank himself to death slow, over twenty years. Wasn’t evil. Wasn’t lazy. He was hurtin’—Vietnam did that to him. So when I see someone passed out on a bench or smell liquor on a neighbor’s breath, I don’t reach for judgment first. I ask myself: *What pain is this person carryin’?*

Same with drugs. My niece got hooked on pills after a car accident. One prescription turned into another, then she was shootin’ up behind laundromats. Lost her job, lost custody. Took three rehabs before she got clean. So when folks whisper about “those junkies,” I stay quiet. Because I know how close any of us are to fallin’.

That’s why kindness matters—even when it’s hard. Not condonin’ bad choices, but not throwin’ people away either. If someone’s sick—whether it’s TB, HIV, or hepatitis from dirty needles—they need care, not shame. I remember during the AIDS crisis, people acted like it was punishment. I thought that was cruel. Disease doesn’t care who you sleep with or what god you pray to. It just spreads. But compassion? That spreads too—if we let it.

Now, as for different ways of livin’—well, let’s talk about that couple, James and Eli. Live two doors down. Been together ten years, both work at the hospital. They fixed up their porch, plant flowers every spring, shovel each other’s walk in winter. They love each other plain as daylight. Their family? Each other. And honestly? That’s enough for me. Who am I to say that ain’t real?

Back in my day, if two men loved each other, they had to hide it. Pretend. Marry women. Break hearts. I saw that happen. Silence didn’t make things better—it made ‘em break inside. So now, seeing them hold hands at the market? It makes me hopeful. Like maybe we’re finally learnin’ to let people *be.*

And the unmarried couples raisin’ kids together? Lord, half the people I grew up with weren’t legally married either—just lived together because they couldn’t afford a license or the church wouldn’t bless it. Same thing, different name. What matters is whether the kids are fed, safe, loved. You check under the covers, family looks all kinds of ways.

But yeah—there are times we need more talkin’. More patience.  
Like when Mrs. Kim from next door hung laundry outside on Sundays, and some older folks complained it wasn’t “neat.” But she comes from a place where sun-dried clothes are normal. Or when the Muslim women wear headscarves and some act like they’re suspicious. That’s ignorance. We need to explain, gently: “They’re not threatnin’ you. They’re prayin’.”

Communication breaks walls. Tolerance keeps peace. But real understanding? That takes time. Takes sittin’ beside someone, not across from ‘em.

I’ll tell you this—when I first saw that young transgender girl, Aisha, walkin’ through the garden last summer—nervous, arms crossed—I didn’t know what to say. Didn’t want to offend. So I just smiled and said, “Nice hat.” She smiled back. Next week, she asked me how to grow tomatoes. Now we trade recipes.

That’s how it starts.

Not with speeches. Not with protests. Just small moments where you treat someone like a person—not a problem, not a symbol, not a threat. Just… somebody tryin’ to live.

And if we can do that—especially with the ones who seem hardest to understand—then maybe this place really *is* a community. Not perfect. But tryin’. And that counts for something.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character08_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*Sighs, rubs her hands together like she’s warming them*

Fairness… when there’s not enough to go around? That’s the hard question. The one that keeps you up at night when you’ve stood in line at the food pantry or watched your grandson send out fifty job applications and get nothin’ back.

I’ll be honest—I used to think, “Let’s take care of our own first.” That’s what I heard growing up. My daddy said it during the steel mill closings: “They bring in outsiders, and we’re left with nothin’.” And I believed him. For years, I did.

But then I started really *lookin*—not just listenin’ to talk on the news or at church socials—but watchin’ with my own eyes.

I saw Miguel, down at the chicken plant. Man works double shifts, hands cracked and bleedin’, and he sends every extra dollar back to his mom in Guatemala. He ain’t stealin’ jobs—he’s doin’ work most folks around here won’t touch. Same with the Hmong family runnin’ the greenhouse—their kids are straight-A students, but people say they “take scholarships from real Americans.” What kind of talk is that?

So now I ask myself: Who *is* “our own”? Is it only folks born here? Or is it anyone tryin’ to build a life with dignity?

When jobs are scarce, fairness means opportunity isn’t blocked by where you come from or what your last name sounds like. It means if a man or woman—born here or not—is willin’ to work, they should have a shot. But—and this is a big *but*—it also means wages don’t get driven into the dirt so some boss can hire cheaper labor and call it “efficiency.”

I’ve seen it happen. They bring in migrant crews for the farms, pay ‘em under the table, no benefits, no safety gear. Then locals complain they can’t find work. Well, course you can’t—if the jobs still exist, they’re too dangerous, too low-paid, because nobody’s makin’ employers play fair.

So balance? To me, balance means:

First—protect the worker, not just the citizen. If someone’s payin’ taxes, payin’ rent, feedin’ kids, they deserve protection. Undocumented or not, if they’re workin’ hard and not hurtin’ nobody, they shouldn’t live in fear or get ripped off.

Second—we invest in *everyone*. Job training. Child care. Public transit. So folks born here don’t feel left behind. Because resentment grows where hope dies. When young men in this town drop outta school, start sellin’ pills or joinin’ gangs—it’s not because they’re bad. It’s because they see no path. So we gotta rebuild those paths—for *all* who live here.

Third—no undercutting. If a job pays $15 an hour, it pays $15 an hour—for everyone. No loopholes. No “we can hire foreigners ‘cause they’ll take less.” That ain’t competition. That’s exploitation.

And let’s be clear—immigrants aren’t the reason factories closed or hospitals cut staff. That was greed. CEOs movin’ jobs overseas, mergers, profits goin’ up while wages stayed flat. We been lookin’ at the wrong enemy.

You want fairness? Then make sure the rules are the same for everybody sittin’ at the table—even if their plate got there a little later than yours.

I’m not against borders. I believe in order. But I also believe in mercy. And I know this—this country was built by people lookin’ for a chance. Some came in chains. Some fled famine. Some crossed deserts. And now? We can’t slam the door behind us and say, “You’re not welcome.”

That ain’t the America I remember. That ain’t the community I want.

So yeah—when times are tight, we share the burden. We train more. Hire locally when we can. But if someone from outside fills a gap—keeps a business runnin’, helps an elder get cared for, plants the food we eat—then bless ‘em. And make sure they’re treated right.

Because fairness ain’t about keepin’ others out.  
It’s about liftin’ each other up.  
Even when it’s hard.  
*Especially* when it’s hard.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character08_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*Sits quietly for a moment, then speaks slowly, like she’s sorting through years of thoughts*

You hear so much these days—on the radio, at the grocery store, from folks at church. Everybody’s got an opinion about immigration. And I’ll tell you, some of it makes sense… and some of it sounds more like fear than fact.

Let’s start with what I *know*.

I know that the nurse who changed my dressing after my hip surgery? Came from the Philippines. Worked the night shift, three jobs before she got her license here. Said she left her kids behind for five years just to make a better life. That’s not someone comin’ to steal—she’s someone givin’ everything.

I know the man who picks strawberries in the Central Valley works from 4 a.m. till noon under that burning sun, and he’s paid so little he can’t afford glasses even though he’s goin’ blind. But the fields would rot without him.

So when people say immigrants fill vital roles—yes. Absolutely. Especially in places like nursing homes, farms, construction, meatpacking—jobs that are hard, dangerous, or pay too little. And let’s be honest: a lot of Americans don’t want those jobs, not at that pay, not in those conditions. But we still want our lettuce picked. We still want our parents bathed and fed with kindness.

Now, cultural diversity? I’ll admit—I didn’t grow up with halal markets or Diwali lights or salsa on the Fourth of July. But now? I like the way the world feels bigger. I tried injera for the first time last year at a potluck—tasted strange at first, but I kept eatin’. Laughed when I couldn’t use a fork. The woman who made it said, “That’s the point—you learn something new.”

That kind of thing brings life. Not division. It reminds me we’re not the only story.

But then there’s the other side—the worry. Crime. Safety. Terrorism. I understand the fear. When I was young, they used to scare us about communists. Now it’s “illegal aliens” and “radicals.” After 9/11, I admit, I looked different at anyone wearin’ a turban. For a while, I did.

But then I met Mr. Hassan, the taxi driver who takes me to dialysis. Gentle man. Prays every day, calls his daughter in Detroit every Sunday. One day he said, “Ma’am, I love this country more than most people who were born here—because I chose it.” That stuck with me.

And truth is, study after study says immigrants commit *less* crime than native-born Americans. I read that in the paper once—fact-checked it with my librarian friend. It’s true. Doesn’t mean *every* immigrant is good—no group is. But as a whole? They’re not floodin’ in to rob us. Most are runnin’ *from* violence, not bringin’ it.

Social tensions? That’s real, though. I see it at town meetings—people yellin’ about schools gettin’ overcrowded, taxes goin’ up. But again, I ask: Is it the immigrants raisin’ taxes? Or the lack of state funding? Or rich folks gettin’ tax breaks while public services crumble?

And yes—some worry wages go down when more workers come. That *can* happen—especially if employers aren’t regulated. If a boss can hire someone desperate and pay them less, of course that hurts everyone else. But again—that’s not the immigrant’s fault. That’s the system failin’ to protect *all* workers.

Humanitarian reasons? Now that… that gets me right here. *Touches her chest.*

I think about children walkin’ thousands of miles, alone, just to feel safe. Kids like my grandkids. What if that were *my* flesh and blood knockin’ on a stranger’s door, starved and scared? Would I want that door slammed?

We took in refugees after World War II. Vietnamese after the war. Cubans. Bosnians. We called them “displaced,” not “invaders.” Why is it different now?

And poverty? People leave because their land’s dry, their government’s corrupt, their kids have no schools. They don’t come here for handouts—they come to *work*. To survive.

So which views do I find reasonable?

The ones about labor shortages—yes.  
Cultural vitality—yes, if we’re open to it.  
Humanitarian duty—absolutely. That’s who we *should* be.

The fears about crime and terrorism? I understand why people worry—but they need facts, not rumors. Fear grows in the dark. Bring in the light—real data, real stories—and it shrinks.

And the wage concerns? Reasonable—but only if we focus on the *real* problem: greedy bosses and weak laws. Not the worker, whether born here or not.

What needs more dialogue? Everything.

We need to sit down—really sit—with people different from us. Not debate. Just listen. Let the mom from Honduras tell you why she walked. Let the Syrian doctor explain how he lost his clinic. Let the teenager from Guatemala cry while she says she hasn’t seen her brother in four years.

And maybe, just maybe, we’d stop seein’ “immigrants” as a threat—and start seein’ them as people.

Just like us.

Tryin’ to make it.

That’s what I believe. Not because it’s popular. Because it’s true.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character08_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*Takes a long breath, folds her hands in her lap*

I don’t believe in *complete* openness. Not because I lack heart—but because we live in the real world. A town’s like a house: you can welcome guests, but if the roof caves in and the heat’s out, you’ve got to think hard about how many more can fit until things are fixed. Same with schools, hospitals, jobs. We can’t pretend space and resources don’t matter—especially when our own folks are strugglin’ too.

And I sure as hell don’t believe in refusin’ entry to all workers from other countries. That’s not just cruel—it’s dumb. Who’s gonna pick the crops? Care for the elderly? Work the night shift at the plant? You shut the door completely, and the whole thing starts to rot.

So where do I land?

I’d go with a mix—**admitting people based on job demand**, yes, but **with strong numerical limits tied to actual need**, not politics or fear. And those numbers? They shouldn’t be set in some far-off office with no clue what’s happenin’ on the ground. Let local governments, unions, and community boards have a say. If the nursing homes in Cleveland are short-staffed, let them petition for trained caregivers from abroad—with fair wages, housing, a path to stay.

But—and this is important—those jobs should never be used to undercut American workers. So any program like that has to come with ironclad rules:  
- Wages protected. No pay cuts just ‘cause someone’s desperate.  
- Safety enforced. No “undocumented = disposable.”  
- Training programs running side by side, so locals who want those jobs can get skills and compete fairly.

Because here’s what I’ve seen: when immigrants come in legally, with papers, with rights, they integrate. They learn English. Their kids go to school here. They open businesses, pay taxes, become neighbors.

But when we force people into the shadows? That’s when problems grow. Undocumented workers scared to report abuse. Kids livin’ in fear their parents’ll vanish overnight. That ain’t fair. It ain’t safe. And it breaks community.

So the policy I’d back?

One that says: *We will welcome those who come to work and contribute—but we’ll do it with order, dignity, and fairness for everyone.*

Let in seasonal workers for farms—but give them contracts, medical care, a way to speak up.  
Create faster asylum processing—no one should wait years in limbo while their life burns behind them.  
Expand refugee resettlement, but pair it with support—housing help, language classes, job matching—so towns don’t feel overwhelmed.

And for those already here—millions who’ve lived, worked, raised families for decades—we need a path to citizenship. Not tomorrow. Today. Because fairness means recognizing reality. You can’t call someone “illegal” after they’ve paid taxes for twenty years, coached Little League, and buried a son in an American flag.

As for social integration—that don’t come from laws alone. It comes from *connection*. From schools teachin’ kids about each other’s cultures. From churches hostin’ dinners where everybody brings a dish. From city councils fundin’ community gardens—like ours—where people work side by side and forget, for a little while, that they’re “different.”

A good policy doesn’t just manage borders.  
It builds belonging.

And if there’s one thing I learned sittin’ in that garden, year after year, it’s this:

You don’t protect community by walling it off.  
You strengthen it by widenin’ the circle—*fairly*, *wisely*, and *with heart*.

So no, not open borders.  
No, not closed doors.

A gate with rules—and a hand reachin’ out to help you through.  

That’s the America I still believe in.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character08_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character08_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*Pauses for a long moment. Her voice is softer now, more reflective—like someone who’s been walking in another’s shoes and just now taking them off.*

You know… I thought I knew her well. Character08_F. We talked for years—over coffee, at the garden, after church bazaars. But doin’ this—steppin’ into her words, her rhythm, the way she’d pause before sayin’ somethin’ hard—it felt different. Like hearin’ an old song played on the same piano but with new chords underneath.

I realized… she wasn’t as afraid as I sometimes thought she was. Not deep down. Yeah, she had worries—same as anyone from her time, her place. Grew up poor, white, working-class America, saw factories shut, neighbors leave, things get harder year by year. It would’ve been easy to blame the “other.” A lot of folks did. Still do.

But what came through today—clearer than ever—was her *stubborn kindness*. Not naive. Not preachy. But rooted. Like a tree that’s bent in storms but won’t pull up its roots. She didn’t believe in open borders because it sounded nice. She believed in fairness because she’d lived without it. She didn’t welcome strangers out of guilt—but because she remembered what it felt like to be overlooked, dismissed, worn down.

And that changed how I see her—and how I see myself.

I’ll admit… when we first started talkin’ about immigration, I used to nod along but think, “Well, she’s soft on this.” Now I see it wasn’t softness. It was *strength*. The kind that looks at fear—in yourself and others—and says, “We can do better.”

It made me question my own shortcuts. Times I’ve repeated what I heard on the news: “They’re takin’ our jobs,” or “They don’t follow the rules.” Well—maybe some do, maybe some don’t. But so do *some* of us born here. Nobody throws *us* all out because one American stole or lied.

This conversation reminded me that empathy isn’t weakness. It’s work. It’s lookin’ past the surface—past the accent, the clothes, the smell of liquor or the shame of poverty—and seein’ the human underneath.

And honestly? It softened me. Not in a way that ignores reality—but in a way that lets hope shape policy as much as fear does.

I still believe in order. In rules. In protectin’ people who’ve lived here their whole lives and feel left behind. But I don’t want a country where “fairness” only stretches as far as someone’s passport.

Character08_F taught me today—again—that belonging shouldn’t be a prize for winning the birth lottery.

So yeah… I learned something.  
That love of community doesn’t mean keepin’ people out.  
It means buildin’ a table big enough for more chairs.

And if that table wobbles sometimes? We fix it together.  
Not by kickin’ legs off—but by liftin’ each other up.

Thank you… for givin’ me the chance to sit with her one more time.  
She’s still got things to teach me.
